units: rainwater does not soak into tarmac surfaces
the quick runoff reaches the watercourse all at once
these sudden arrivals push the river out of its bed
the banks lose their fine sediment to the current
bare cultivated ground wears away in the same manner
perforated slabs replace the tarmac of car parks
sown cover crops open root channels that soak up the downpour
planted ditches store the runoff before handing it back to the subsoil
text: Rain that lands on tarmac has nowhere to go. It skims across the surface, fills the drains and reaches the watercourse in one sudden shove. That surge lifts the river out of its bed, and the current strips the fine silt from the banks as it goes. Bare ploughed land wears away much the same, because the downpour hits a packed crust that no root holds together. The remedies that exist all come back to a single idea: give the ground its thirst back. Planners are pulling up the tarmac in car parks and laying perforated slabs that grass can settle into. Growers sow a cover crop between harvests, and those roots bore channels that drink the downpour. Elsewhere, shallow ditches planted with reeds hold the runoff for a while, then hand it back unhurriedly to the water table underground.

units: the narrator returns to a jetty she knew as a child
she remembers damp, quiet air on her early visits
the fierce wind of her recent visit nearly tore her bag away
sheets of water were now coming over the low wall
the lighthouse keeper describes storms closer together than before
he once counted a single serious warning each season
he now counts three or four between two big tides
the narrator finds that the place of her childhood has changed character
text: I went back to the harbour jetty during the storm season, and I could barely place the spot. As a girl I used to walk out there through a soft, salty haze, with the damp settling on my cheeks and nothing much stirring. This time a gust nearly ripped the bag off my shoulder, and sheets of water were coming clean over the low wall. The lighthouse keeper told me the blows land closer together now, with far deeper troughs behind them. He used to log one bad warning a season, he said; these days he counts three or four between one big tide and the next. It is not the same coast any more, honestly. The sand has thinned by the steps, the fishermen have shifted their pots into the shelter of the pier, and the place I grew up with feels like an out-of-date map you keep out of fondness.

units: a household compost bin fits into a small space
the method falls into three parts
the bin must stand on living soil, out of full sun
wet waste and dry material have to be alternated
meat scraps are kept out of the mixture
the heap must be turned at regular intervals to air it
a dampness like that of a wrung-out sponge is what you want
the end product is a dark, crumbly material that feeds the soil
text: Composting at home takes up less room than most people expect, and the job splits neatly into three parts. The bin first: stand a slatted container straight on living soil, in the light shade of a hedge, so that worms can climb up into it. Then the material: layer wet stuff, peelings or grass clippings, with dry stuff, fallen leaves or torn brown card. Keep meat scraps out, since they draw in rodents and stall the whole process. Upkeep last: turn the heap with a fork every fortnight and check that it stays as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Too wet and it starts to stink; too dry and it goes to sleep. After two seasons you are left with a dark, crumbly material, not far off the humus of a woodland floor, which you spread around your plantings to feed the soil and hold the water in.

units: an embankment gave way before sunrise
a man on the night shift was the first to raise the alarm
the residents left with very little in their hands
the water reached the first floor of the low houses
the current fell away in the second half of the following night
a grey silt covered the streets once the water had gone
the rescue teams set pumps down on the central square
an engineer blames the failure on runoff from the hillsides
text: The embankment gave way a little before dawn, quietly, the way a seam lets go. A man on the night shift watched it open from the footbridge and set off the siren. Thick mist still lay over the village when people came out with a bag apiece, leaving their kitchen lights burning behind them. The flood climbed to the first floor of the low houses, held that level right through the night that followed, then began to slacken. What it left as it drew back was a grey silt, smooth as varnish, poured along the streets. The rescue teams set their pumps down on the central square, and the drone of the engines took the place of the water's silence. An engineer from the rivers office puts the failure down to the runoff off the stripped hillsides, which loaded the channel far beyond its designed measure.

units: the treeless plateau sheds its heat as soon as the sun goes
the heat stored in the ground leaves towards a clear sky
the air against the ground falls below its dew point
the water vapour then settles as beads on the plants
a deposit of crystals forms once the surface drops below freezing
that frozen deposit draws a white fringe along the edge of the leaves
cold air gathers in the hollows of the ground
the dips therefore freeze before the slopes that stand above them
text: On this bare, treeless plateau the surface begins shedding heat the moment the sun drops away. The ground has taken in energy through the sunlit hours, and it gives that energy up to a cloudless sky, which sends none of it back. So the layer of air lying against the ground cools faster than the air above it. Once that layer falls past its dew point, the vapour it carries can no longer stay hidden: it settles as fine beads on stems and spiders' webs, and that is dew. Should the surface drop below freezing, the deposit changes character and turns to frost, a white fringe of crystals along the edge of every leaf. Cold air, being heavier than mild air, then slides down the slopes and gathers in the hollows. The dips whiten well before the ground above them, at much the same height.

units: the author holds it unreasonable to cover fertile ground with buildings
a productive soil takes thousands of years to assemble
a mineral covering removes that resource with no way back
built surfaces make flooding worse downstream
the author would make each further development conditional on reclaiming a brownfield
he asks that the price of a plot take in its capacity to feed people
he wants the stripping of abandoned ground made compulsory
he holds these measures to be administrative rather than technological
text: It is hard to defend the habit of building over our most fertile ground without ever pricing what is lost. A productive soil takes thousands of years to assemble, one thread of humus at a time, and a concrete slab cancels it within a single building season. The loss is not merely agricultural: sealed surfaces throw the rainfall downstream, where it feeds the flooding that the towns then pay dearly to repair. Three measures would be enough to turn this around. Make each further development conditional on bringing an already built brownfield back into use. Write into the value of a plot its capacity to feed people, rather than its suitability for construction alone. Finally, require that abandoned sites be stripped back, so the subsoil is returned to the water. These are levers of public decision, not feats of engineering still waiting to be invented.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the warden looks after a waterlogged marsh
she reads the height of the water off graduated rules
she likens her work to that of a nurse
she explains that a patient and a marsh are both treated by small corrections
the man before her set out above all to drain the site
she has had the old drainage ditches blocked
the spongy growth came back after that work
the marsh now holds the water of heavy rain
text: The warden of a marsh at the bottom of a valley spends her weeks watching a soil that breathes. Graduated rules stand planted in the peat, and she reads the water off them, feels the moss between her fingers, listens for the frogs. She describes the work as a nurse's: you do not cure anyone by shaking them, you adjust, you watch, you go round again. That comparison also lights up what separates her from the man before her. He wanted the place drained, the ditches cut straight, the acreage won back for crops; she has had those channels blocked one by one. The spongy moss grew back, the brown layer thickened, and the floor of the valley began once more to drink the downpours instead of flinging them at the village below. She says the job has taught her a patience she never knew she had.

units: the visitor expected nothing of this exhibition on the climate
she came out of it thrilled
a first room throws a fine spray of water over the visitors
a great fan there works up a storm wind
a second room shows hailstones kept in the cold
a third room smells of damp woodland
the visitor finds the explanatory panels too crowded
she recommends the visit in spite of that flaw
text: Honestly, I expected nothing at all from this exhibition on the climate, and I came out of it thrilled. Three rooms, three ideas, and not a dull stretch anywhere in the place. The first one soaks you: jets throw out a salty spray while a great fan works up a gale, and you grasp at once what a battered coast puts up with. The second plays on cold. Behind a frosted pane lie hailstones collected after a thunderstorm, big as walnuts, sliced open to show the concentric rings inside them. The third goes for the nose: you step into a rebuilt patch of woodland smelling of wet moss, while a blower pushes the scent of leaf mould at you. My one complaint is with the panels, wordy and cramped, which nobody is going to read standing up. Do go anyway, and save some breath for the last room.

units: the writer sends her cousin news of a stream
the watercourse had been shut inside a concrete pipe
a group of neighbours won its return to the open air
the machines opened the pipe at the start of the cold season
willows and rushes were planted along the banks
heavy rain arrived before the young plants had rooted
the banks held despite that rise in the water
dragonflies have been seen over the reopened stream
text: Dear cousin, you asked for news of the stream, so here is how the season went. It started when the neighbours' group finally won the right to open the watercourse up again, after decades shut away inside a concrete pipe. The machines came in with the cold weather and split the slab along the whole length of the common meadow. We planted willows and rushes on the banks, mud up to our knees, and by the second week the water had found its winding line again. Then a violent downpour arrived before the roots had taken hold, and we were sure we had lost the lot; the banks held, barely nicked. Since then dragonflies patrol above the pebbles, and the children from the hamlet come hunting for larvae under the flat stones. Come and see us before the snow patches melt, you will not know the meadow.

units: the moisture laid on the leaves comes from the air itself
the night-time cooling of surfaces brings about that deposit
air loaded with vapour can no longer hold it in suspension
mist forms when the condensation happens in the air rather than on a surface
a cover of cloud stops the deposit from happening
ground rich in organic matter holds more moisture
that moisture keeps alive the organisms which break down plant debris
taking away the plant cover dries out the reserve
text: What lays that moisture on the leaves before daybreak? Nothing has fallen from the sky: the air has simply surrendered what it held. Shedding heat into the emptiness of the night, a plant's surface grows colder than the surrounding air, and the invisible vapour condenses there. That is dew. And if the chilling reaches the entire body of air, not merely a surface? Then the droplets hang where they are, and a mist spreads low across the meadow. A covered sky, by contrast, throws the heat back down and cancels the whole business. Where does the water go? The ground drinks it, all the more readily for being loaded with rotted plant matter. That store sustains the countless creatures gnawing dead leaves back into the earth. Strip off the plant cover, and you dry out the reserve first, then the quiet life depending on it.
